1. Localized oral amyloidosis (amyloidoma) — matches yellowish cobblestone plaques and H&E showing extracellular eosinophilic amorphous subepithelial deposits.
2. Systemic amyloidosis with oral involvement (AL or AA) — similar histology but would require systemic workup to exclude multisystem disease.
3. Granular cell tumor (multiple lesions or multifocal presentation) — can present as yellowish nodules on tongue; histology usually shows granular eosinophilic cells rather than extracellular amorphous material (less likely given current description).
4. Verruciform xanthoma — clinically can be verrucous/yellowish papules with subepithelial foam cells; histology differs but can have cobblestone appearance.
5. Chronic hyperplastic candidiasis /other chronic inflammatory plaques — clinically possible but less likely because lesions do not scrape off and histology favors extracellular deposits rather than fungal elements.

Recommended immediate confirmatory steps (strongly advised): Congo red stain with polarized-light examination of the biopsy (to confirm amyloid) and, if positive, serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light-chain assay plus basic organ evaluation (CBC, CMP, urinalysis, ECG, and consider echocardiography and renal assessment) to distinguish localized from systemic amyloidosis.
ground_truth: Nodular colloid degeneration of the tongue
